alt: A pull quote reading "Working out the chords by ear is not a single flash of recognition. It is a series of small tests."
caption:
Find a likely home note, follow the bass, try the common chords around it, and go back to the bar
that still sounds wrong. A practical method for the songs nobody has charted.

alt: The chords C, A minor, F and G set large above the Roman numerals one, six minor, four, five.
caption:
C–Am–F–G is the doo-wop turnaround: four bars that circle straight back to the start, which is
why so many fifties and sixties songs sit on it for a whole verse.

Chord symbols above, Roman numerals below — today's post is about when to reach for which:
chordlist.app/blog/chord-notation-styles

alt: The chords G, D, E minor and C set large above the Roman numerals one, five, six minor, four.
caption:
G–D–Em–C turns up often enough that learning it cleanly gives your hands and ears a reference for
other songs. It will not unlock every pop song, and that is not the point.

Read the full post: chordlist.app/blog/how-to-play-almost-any-pop-song

alt: A dark chordlist card reading "Your lyrics and chords, as files in your pocket."
caption:
Every song you save is a plain Markdown file in a folder you choose. No account, no export
button, no lock-in — open the same folder in any editor on any device.

chordlist for iPhone and iPad. chordlist.app

alt: A chordlist song detail screen on iPhone listing other songs that share the same chord progression.
caption:
Open a song and chordlist shows you which other songs in your library use the same progression —
the starting point for a mashup, or just an easy second song to play in the same shape.

Today's post covers what counts as a match and how to turn the results into a setlist:
chordlist.app/blog/finding-songs-that-share-a-progression

alt: A dark chordlist card reading "No account. No upload. Just a folder."
caption:
chordlist does not upload or sync your song library. You pick the folder through the Files
picker, and if that folder happens to be in iCloud Drive, it is Apple's file service doing the
syncing — not us.

chordlist.app/privacy

alt: A pull quote reading "Obsidian sees notes and folders. chordlist sees artists and songs."
caption:
One iCloud folder can be an Obsidian vault and a chordlist library at the same time. Write and
organise in Obsidian, open the same files in chordlist when you play. Neither app needs a
converted copy.

Read the full post: chordlist.app/blog/one-folder-obsidian-and-chordlist

alt: A dark chordlist card reading "There is no export button. There is nothing to export."
caption:
An export turns your library into a second copy that has to keep working. When every song starts
as an ordinary Markdown file, copying the folder is the export.

chordlist.app/faq

alt: The chords A, D and E set large above the Roman numerals one, four, five.
caption:
The twelve-bar blues spends four bars on the I, two on the IV, two more on the I, then one each
on the V and IV before turning around. Three chords, arranged in time.

alt: The chords D minor, G and C set large above the Roman numerals two minor, five, one.
caption:
ii–V–I is the standard way home in jazz, and it works the same in any key: the ii sets up the V,
and the V resolves. Learn it in C, then move it.
